title: Irus (Arnaeus), the town beggar
greek: Ἀρναῖος δ᾽ ὄνομ᾽ ἔσκε ... Ἶρον δὲ νέοι κίκλησκον ἅπαντες (Arnaios d' onom' eske ... Iron de neoi kiklēskon hapantes)
short: The public beggar's real name was Arnaeus; the young men nicknamed him Irus because he ran errands, like the messenger goddess Iris.
body: Monro explains the nickname as a masculine form of Iris, the gods' messenger in the Iliad: Irus 'used to run on errands when anyone bade him'. His mother's name for him, Arnaeus, gives him the dignity of a proper birth name, which the community has replaced with a joke. He is a parody of Odysseus' disguise: a real 'public beggar' (ptōchos pandēmios), huge in bulk but without strength, defending his patch against the newcomer. Critics have long seen Iliadic models behind the episode. Steiner, as her reviewers note, traces allusions to the boxing match of Iliad XXIII and to Thersites, the ugly commoner whom Odysseus beats in Iliad II. The burlesque fight lets Odysseus display his strength while still appearing to be a beggar, and gives the suitors a first glimpse of what is coming.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.6
Bruce Louden, review of Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII, Exemplaria Classica 15 (2011) 323-5 (on the Iliadic lens of the Irus episode)

title: 'Irus un-Irused' (Iros Airos)
greek: ἦ τάχα Ἶρος Ἄϊρος ἐπίσπαστον κακὸν ἕξει (ē tacha Iros Airos epispaston kakon hexei)
short: A pun with a negative prefix: Irus will soon be 'no-Irus', no longer fit to run errands, having brought trouble on himself.
body: The suitors' joke adds the privative a- ('un-', 'not') to the beggar's own name. Monro glosses Airos as 'Irus no more', no longer fit to be their messenger. Homer uses this kind of name-negating compound for bitter effect elsewhere: Hector calls his brother Dysparis, 'evil Paris' (Il. 3.39), Penelope speaks of Kakoilion, 'evil Ilios' (19.260), and Telemachus calls his mother dysmētēr, 'mother no mother' (23.97). The adjective epispaston, 'drawn upon himself', underlines that Irus has invited his fate by challenging the stranger. The joke is also unwittingly about the suitors: they too will soon have 'drawn evil upon themselves'.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.73

title: The prize: goats' paunches stuffed with fat and blood
greek: γαστέρες αἵδ᾽ αἰγῶν κέατ᾽ ἐν πυρί, τὰς ἐπὶ δόρπῳ κατθέμεθα κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος ἐμπλήσαντες (gasteres haid' aigōn keat' en puri ... knisēs te kai haimatos emplēsantes)
short: Antinous offers a blood-sausage as the prize for the beggars' fight: a comic counterpart to the prizes of heroic games.
body: The gasteres are goats' stomachs stuffed with fat and blood and roasted, something like a black pudding or haggis. The prize is a pun on the theme of the belly (gastēr): two beggars driven by their bellies fight for a belly. Reviewers of Steiner's commentary note her reading of the match as a parody of the funeral games of Iliad XXIII, where the boxing prize is a mule and a two-handled cup (23.653-6); here the 'anti-heroic' prize is food. Antinous adds a second prize: the winner will be the house's sole beggar. The image returns in Book XX, where Odysseus, sleepless, tosses 'like a paunch full of fat and blood' turned before the fire (20.25-30). The man who won the paunch has become one.

sources.cite: Donald Lateiner, review of Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII, Classical Journal Online 2011.12.03 (reporting Steiner's notes on the prize)

title: The boxing match with Irus
greek: ἀνασχομένω (anaschomenō, 'both raising their hands')
short: Athena enlarges Odysseus' limbs; he chooses a measured blow under the ear so as not to reveal himself by killing the beggar.
body: Monro notes the Iliadic phrasing throughout. The formula for the winner, 'whichever proves the better man', is taken from the duel of Paris and Menelaus (Il. 3.71), and 'raising their hands' is the regular boxing term (Il. 23.660). When Odysseus girds up his rags, the sight of his thighs, shoulders and chest is enough to terrify Irus, and Athena 'made greater the limbs of the shepherd of the people', a phrase that gives the beggar a king's epithet. As in the Melanthius scene, the hero debates two courses: a killing blow or a light one. He chooses restraint, 'that the Achaeans might not take note of him', and still smashes the jaw. He then drags Irus out and props him against the courtyard wall with a staff, a prophetic tableau that Telemachus will wish upon all the suitors (18.235-42).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.65, 18.95, 18.100
Bruce Louden, review of Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII, Exemplaria Classica 15 (2011) 323-5 (on the Iliadic lens of the Irus episode)

title: King Echetus, 'bane of all mortals'
greek: εἰς Ἔχετον βασιλῆα, βροτῶν δηλήμονα πάντων (eis Echeton basilēa, brotōn dēlēmona pantōn)
short: A cruel king on the mainland, used by the suitors as a bogeyman threat; ancient commentators placed him in Epirus.
body: Echetus appears only as a threat (18.85, 18.116, 21.308): beggars and offenders will be shipped to him to have their noses and ears cut off and their genitals torn out for the dogs. The scholia made him a tyrant of Epirus (or of the 'Sikeloi'), and later stories gave him a cruel family history, but Monro judges him 'purely imaginary', the bogeyman ('Croquemitaine') of the Odyssey. The threats are revealing: the suitors speak of mutilation and of selling men abroad (compare 20.382-3) with casual relish. Their language anticipates, in reverse, the punishment that Melanthius suffers in Book XXII (22.474-7), where exactly these mutilations are inflicted on the suitors' ally.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.85 and 20.383

title: 'Nothing feebler than man': the warning to Amphinomus
greek: οὐδὲν ἀκιδνότερον γαῖα τρέφει ἀνθρώποιο (ouden akidnoteron gaia trephei anthrōpoio)
short: Odysseus' meditation on human frailty: a man's mind changes with each day Zeus sends, so he should take the gods' gifts in silence.
body: Speaking to the kindest of the suitors, Odysseus offers the poem's most explicit piece of wisdom. Men think themselves secure while the gods give them prosperity; when misfortune comes they bear it unwillingly; 'the mind of men upon the earth is such as the day which the father of gods and men brings upon them' (18.136-7). Monro notes that the archaic poet Archilochus imitated these lines (fr. 131-2 West). The thought echoes Zeus in the Iliad, who calls man the most wretched of all creatures that breathe (Il. 17.446-7). Odysseus then turns his own invented life into an example: he too was lawless, trusting in his strength. The speech is a final, sincere warning: 'mayest thou not meet him when he comes home'. Amphinomus understands enough to be troubled, but does not leave.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.133-8 (with the imitation by Archilochus)

title: Amphinomus 'bound' by Athena
greek: ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ὣς φύγε κῆρα· πέδησε δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἀθήνη (all' oud' hōs phuge kēra; pedēse de kai ton Athēnē)
short: The decent suitor goes away 'boding bane', yet Athena 'shackles' him to his fate: he will die by Telemachus' spear.
body: The verb pedaō means to fetter or shackle (pedē, 'fetter'). In the Iliad it describes fate holding a doomed man fast: 'deadly fate shackled Hector to remain there' outside the gates (Il. 22.5). Amphinomus is the most sympathetic of the suitors. He opposed the plot to kill Telemachus (16.394-405; 20.240-6), he greets the beggar kindly, and he receives Odysseus' warning. Yet he is killed among the first, by Telemachus' spear in the back (22.89-96). The narrator's comment states openly the problem raised by Athena's test (17.360-4): the revenge makes no distinctions. Some readers take this as a flaw in the poem's justice; others as a mark of its tragic realism, in which an individual's good nature cannot save him from the community he has chosen.

title: Penelope's 'meaningless laugh' (achreion egelasse)
greek: ἀχρεῖον δ᾽ ἐγέλασσεν (achreion d' egelassen)
short: An enigmatic laugh as Penelope decides to show herself to the suitors: forced, embarrassed or unaccountable, according to interpreters.
body: Achreios means 'useless' or 'without purpose'. Monro explains the phrase as a 'needless', pointless or forced laugh, comparing the later word achreiogelōs, 'untimely laugher', in the comic poet Cratinus. The only other Homeric use is of Thersites, who after Odysseus beats him 'looked achreion', helpless or foolish (Il. 2.269). Commentators have read the laugh as embarrassment at an impulse she does not understand (since Athena has put the idea in her heart), as a nervous cover for a calculated plan, or as self-mockery at the thought of showing herself to men she hates. The moment is the most discussed of the many laughs in Book XVIII, and its ambiguity is part of the larger debate over Penelope's motives in the scene that follows.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.163

anchor: to show herself to the wooers
title: Penelope shows herself to the suitors
greek: μνηστήρεσσι φανῆναι, ὅπως πετάσειε μάλιστα θυμὸν μνηστήρων (mnēstēressi phanēnai, hopōs petaseie malista thumon mnēstērōn)
short: Prompted by Athena, Penelope appears in the hall, announces that remarriage is near and extracts gifts: one of the poem's great interpretive puzzles.
body: Athena's purpose is stated: to 'flutter' the suitors' hearts and make Penelope 'more honoured' by husband and son. Penelope then recalls Odysseus' parting command to remarry when their son was grown, rebukes the suitors for devouring the house instead of bringing gifts, and receives a robe, jewels and a necklace. Odysseus rejoices that 'she drew gifts from them ... but her mind was set on other things' (18.281-3). Analyst critics (Wilamowitz, Seeck) found the scene inconsistent with Penelope's character and with its context; Monro, after reviewing them, inclines to think it an addition, though he defends Odysseus' trust in her as true to nature. Modern readers have instead explored its ambiguity: Penelope as shrewd strategist, as a woman responding intuitively to her husband's presence, or as a character whom the poet keeps deliberately uncertain. Steiner treats this indeterminacy as part of the design.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.158-303 and 18.281-3
Deborah Steiner, Homer: Odyssey Books XVII and XVIII (Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics; Cambridge, 2010), Introduction, pp. 25-8 (Penelope), as summarised in B. Spence, BMCR 2011.04.58
Marylin A. Katz, Penelope's Renown: Meaning and Indeterminacy in the Odyssey (Princeton, 1991)

title: Athena beautifies the sleeping Penelope
greek: κάλλεϊ μέν οἱ πρῶτα προσώπατα καλὰ κάθηρεν ἀμβροσίῳ (kallei men hoi prōta prosōpata kala kathēren ambrosiōi)
short: While Penelope sleeps, Athena cleans her face with Aphrodite's divine cosmetic, makes her taller and 'whiter than new-sawn ivory'.
body: The goddess uses kallos, here, Monro notes, in the concrete sense of a beauty-ointment, the ambrosial one that Aphrodite ('Cytherea of the fair crown') applies before dancing with the Graces. Penelope is made taller and fuller and given an ivory-white complexion, the ideal of female beauty for women who stay indoors. The scene is a divine toilette like Hera's before she seduces Zeus (Il. 14.166-86) and Aphrodite's after her escape to Paphos (Od. 8.362-6). Athena's similar transformations of Odysseus (6.229-35; 23.156-62) make the couple's beauty a matched gift. Penelope sleeps through the whole process and wakes wishing for death, so the beauty is put on her rather than chosen by her.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.190-6

anchor: knees of the wooers were loosened
title: 'Their knees were loosened': desire and death
greek: τῶν δ᾽ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατ᾽, ἔρῳ δ᾽ ἄρα θυμὸν ἔθελχθεν (tōn d' autou luto gounat', erōi d' ara thumon ethelchthen)
short: The formula for a man struck down in battle, used here of desire: the suitors' knees go weak at the sight of Penelope.
body: In the Iliad 'his knees were loosened' is a standard way of saying a warrior was killed or overcome by fear. Hesiod calls Eros the 'limb-loosener' (lusimelēs, Theogony 120-1), and later lyric poets use the same image for love's power over the body. Here the two meanings meet, and the irony is grim: the first half of this line returns at 22.68, when Odysseus has thrown off his rags and the suitors' 'knees were loosened and their hearts' in terror. Their 'enchanted' hearts (ethelchthen, from thelgein) also recall the language of song and magic (17.514, 17.521). The scene of desire thus anticipates the scene of death in the same hall.

title: Iasian Argos
greek: ἀν᾽ Ἴασον Ἄργος Ἀχαιοί (an' Iason Argos Achaioi)
short: An old poetic name, found only here, for the Peloponnese or for Greece as a whole, probably after Iasus, a legendary king of Argos.
body: Monro notes that the phrase occurs only here and must mean the whole Peloponnese, if not all Greece; it is 'one of the old geographical names that survive in poetical tradition', sometimes after their first meaning was forgotten. The epithet is usually connected with Iasus, an early king of Argos and father of Io in the genealogies reported by Pausanias (2.16.1). Monro mentions, and doubts, E. Curtius' attempt to link it with Ionians in the early Peloponnese. Eurymachus' flattery is therefore expansive: if all the Achaeans of the whole land could see Penelope, still more suitors would come. Penelope's reply turns the compliment aside by speaking of her lost husband.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.246

anchor: see my son a bearded man
title: Odysseus' parting instruction: remarry when our son is bearded
greek: αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ παῖδα γενειήσαντα ἴδηαι, γήμασθ᾽ ᾧ κ᾽ ἐθέλῃσθα (autar epēn dē paida geneiēsanta idēai, gēmasth' hōi k' ethelēistha)
short: Penelope reveals that Odysseus himself set the condition for her remarriage, and that the condition has now been met.
body: This is the only place where we hear Odysseus' farewell to his wife. Holding her right wrist, he foresaw that he might not return, entrusted his parents to her care, and gave her a time limit: when she saw their son grown and bearded, she might marry whom she pleased. Eurynome has just reminded Penelope that Telemachus is now 'a bearded man' (18.175-6), and Monro, following Seeck, sees the comparison of these two passages as the key to the scene: Penelope is announcing that the end of her resistance has come. The speech gives her decision legitimacy, since she obeys her husband even in remarrying, and it raises the stakes for the contest she will propose in Book XIX (19.570-81).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.158-303 (comparison of 18.176 and 18.269)

title: Proper wooing: cattle, feasts and gifts
greek: αὐτοὶ τοί γ᾽ ἀπάγουσι βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα, κούρης δαῖτα φίλοισι, καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα διδοῦσιν (autoi toi g' apagousi boas kai iphia mēla, kourēs daita philoisi, kai aglaa dōra didousin)
short: Penelope reminds the suitors that rivals for a bride should give feasts and gifts, not consume the bride's household.
body: Homeric marriage involves exchanges whose exact nature is disputed. Suitors compete by offering hedna, bride-gifts, usually to the bride's family (Il. 16.178-90; Od. 15.16-18), yet some passages speak of hedna provided by the bride's father, closer to a dowry (Od. 1.277-8 = 2.196-7). M. I. Finley read these exchanges as gift-giving between households; Anthony Snodgrass argued that the inconsistencies show the poems mixing customs from different periods. Penelope's appeal is to the essential principle: wooers should bring wealth, not take it 'without atonement'. Monro stresses the serious importance of gift customs in Homeric society. The suitors comply at once with a robe with twelve golden brooches, an amber necklace 'bright as the sun', earrings and a jewel, and Odysseus rejoices to see his wife enriching the house at their expense.

sources.cite: M. I. Finley, 'Marriage, Sale and Gift in the Homeric World', Revue internationale des droits de l'antiquité, 3rd ser., 2 (1955) 167-94
A. M. Snodgrass, 'An Historical Homeric Society?', Journal of Hellenic Studies 94 (1974) 114-25
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.282 and 18.294-8

title: The braziers and the beggar as torch-bearer
greek: αὐτίκα λαμπτῆρας τρεῖς ἵστασαν ἐν μεγάροισιν (autika lamptēras treis histasan en megaroisin)
short: Fire-pans light the hall at night; Odysseus sends the maids away and takes over the task of keeping them burning.
body: Lamptēres are braziers, open metal pans set on stands and fed with dry wood; in the spaces between them, Monro explains, attendants held torches and relieved one another in turns (compare the golden torch-bearing statues in Alcinous' palace, 7.100-2). Odysseus offers to do the work himself, saying that he 'can endure much', and stands by the braziers watching the men while 'his heart pondered other things'. Monro rightly values 'the striking picture of Ulysses acting himself as the unwearied torch-bearer'. The image is charged with irony. The master of the house serves as its lamp-stand, Eurymachus will joke that the light comes from his bald head (18.353-5), and the light he tends is the light by which the suitors will die.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.307-11 and 18.343

title: Melantho, the disloyal maid
greek: Μελανθὼ καλλιπάρῃος (Melanthō kallipārēios)
short: Daughter of Dolius, raised by Penelope, mistress of Eurymachus: the leader of the maids who side with the suitors.
body: Melantho is the sister of the goatherd Melanthius, and like his her name contains melas, 'black'. The narrator gives her a short, damning biography: Penelope reared her like a daughter and gave her toys, but she has no pity for her mistress and sleeps with Eurymachus. She abuses the stranger twice (18.326-36; 19.65-9), suggesting he sleep at the smithy, and is twice rebuked, once by Odysseus and once by Penelope, who calls her a 'shameless dog' (19.91). She is presumably among the twelve maids whom Telemachus hangs after the slaughter (22.461-73). The episode has drawn modern attention to the fate of the slave women, most famously in Margaret Atwood's novella The Penelopiad (2005), which gives the hanged maids a chorus of their own.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 17.212 (the names Melanthius and Melantho)

title: The smithy and the leschē
greek: χαλκήϊον ἐς δόμον ἐλθὼν ... ἠέ που ἐς λέσχην (chalkēion es domon elthōn ... ēe pou es leschēn)
short: Places where the poor slept or gathered for warmth: the forge and the public lounge (leschē), mentioned only here in Homer.
body: The forge was the warmest place in an early Greek village, and vagrants slept there in winter. Hesiod gives the same pairing when he warns the farmer not to idle away the cold season 'by the smith's seat and the warm leschē' (Works and Days 493-4). Monro notes that this is the only mention in Homer of the leschē, a public room or portico for talk and shelter that later became a familiar Greek institution; the best-known example is the Leschē of the Cnidians at Delphi, decorated by the painter Polygnotus (Pausanias 10.25.1). Melantho's insult places the beggar among idle talkers, but it also tells us something about how the landless lived in the world of the poem.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.329

title: Eurymachus' joke: the light from the bald head
greek: ἔμπης μοι δοκέει δαίδων σέλας ἔμμεναι αὐτοῦ κὰκ κεφαλῆς, ἐπεὶ οὔ οἱ ἔνι τρίχες οὐδ᾽ ἠβαιαί (empēs moi dokeei daidōn selas emmenai autou kak kephalēs)
short: Mocking a divine sign, Eurymachus says the beggar 'has come by the will of the gods', since the torchlight seems to shine from his hairless head.
body: Monro explains the joke in two stages. First Eurymachus pretends to see a prodigy: the man standing among the torches must be a source of light that only a god's presence could explain. Then he 'improves' it: the light must come from the head itself, since there is no hair to stop it. The humour is cruel, since baldness is part of Athena's disguise (13.399, 13.431), but it is also unknowingly true. The beggar has indeed come 'not without the will of the gods', and divine light will soon shine in the palace when Athena carries her golden lamp before father and son (19.33-43). Like several of the suitors' jokes, it speaks the truth in mockery.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.354-5

title: Odysseus' challenge: mowing, ploughing and fighting
greek: Εὐρύμαχ᾽, εἰ γὰρ νῶϊν ἔρις ἔργοιο γένοιτο (Eurumach', ei gar nōin eris ergoio genoito)
short: Taunted as work-shy, Odysseus imagines contests of mowing, ploughing a four-acre field and fighting in the front rank, and wins all three.
body: Eurymachus offers the beggar wage labour on a farm and sneers that he prefers begging. Odysseus answers with three imagined contests. The first two belong to the world of Hesiod's Works and Days, where 'good strife' (eris) drives neighbour to compete with neighbour in work (Works and Days 11-26): mowing from dawn to dusk without food, and ploughing a straight furrow across a field of four guai (tetraguon), with matched oxen. The third is Iliadic: fighting among the front-rank fighters with shield, spears and helmet. Monro notes that no breastplate is mentioned, as in a similar passage at 14.482. The speech claims for the disguised king every kind of male excellence, agricultural as well as martial, and ends with a threat: if Odysseus came home, the doors would be too narrow for Eurymachus to run through.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.367-77

title: The closing libation
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄγετ᾽, οἰνοχόος μὲν ἐπαρξάσθω δεπάεσσιν, ὄφρα σπείσαντες κατακείομεν οἴκαδ᾽ ἰόντες (all' aget', oinochoos men eparxasthō depaessin, ophra speisantes katakeiomen oikad' iontes)
short: After Eurymachus' missile and the uproar, Amphinomus ends the evening with the customary libation and the suitors go home to bed.
body: Eurymachus throws a footstool at the beggar, who ducks behind Amphinomus, and the stool hits the wine-pourer instead (18.394-8). Telemachus tells the suitors they are 'mad' and should go home. Amphinomus restores order with ritual. Monro explains the procedure: the wine-pourer 'begins' (eparxasthai) by putting a first drop in each cup, which the drinker pours out to the gods, and then fills the cup, going round the company 'stopping at each in succession' (episstadon). A final libation before sleep is a regular Homeric custom (compare 3.332-42; 7.136-8, where the Phaeacians pour to Hermes before going to bed). The scene ends Book XVIII calmly, but the order it restores is temporary: the suitors leave Odysseus alone in the hall to plan their deaths (19.1-2).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 18.418 and 18.425 (and on 3.340)
